prime.problem: The embeddings come out as a (32, 3, 2) block, but the hidden layer's weights want one row of 6 numbers per example. Gluing the pieces together with a copy on every forward pass is clumsy, and it hard-codes the context length.
prime.fits: It follows the embedding lookup (emb = C[X]) and comes right before the hidden layer. It reuses tensor shapes and indexing from the toolkit, and shows what a tensor really is underneath.
expect: storage: one flat block of memory
prime.goal: Explain why emb.view(-1, 6) costs nothing and gives the same numbers as concatenating, and predict when a view will fail.

attend: Which three small numbers per tensor turn a flat block of memory into a (3, 3, 2) grid?
Why are each example's six numbers already adjacent in emb's memory, and in which order?
What does cat have to do that view doesn't, and how often does that happen in training?
What goes wrong with .view after a transpose, and why does .reshape still work?

must: A tensor = storage + shape + strides + offset → element [i, j, k] is found at offset + i·s₀ + j·s₁ + k·s₂ → changing shape and strides re-reads the same memory → .view is free (no copy)
emb has strides (6, 2, 1) → example n's 6 numbers sit together at storage[6n : 6n + 6], character 0 first → view(-1, 6) just declares stride (6, 1) → the same row-of-6 layout cat builds by copying
A view only re-reads memory, never reorders it → after transpose the numbers aren't in row order → .view raises an error → .reshape (or .contiguous()) has to copy
-1 lets PyTorch infer a dimension from the total count (192 ÷ 6 = 32) → the same line handles a batch of 32, all 228,146 examples, or 1 during sampling
elevated: Views share storage → writing through a view changes the original (setting view[0, 0] = 99. sets emb[0, 0, 0]) → harmless in this MLP, a silent bug if you edit a view expecting a copy
reference: torch.unbind(t, dim) returns a tuple of slices along dim
the exact RuntimeError text for an incompatible view
the arange(18) storage is 144 bytes (18 int64s × 8 bytes)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw torch.arange(18) as a strip of 18 slots, then mark how view(3, 3, 2) reads it. Or explain in 3–5 sentences why emb.view(-1, 6) equals the cat version but costs nothing.
checklist: a tensor is a header (shape, strides, offset) over a flat storage
stride = slots to skip per step along a dimension; address = offset + Σ index × stride
emb's last two dims are already contiguous per example, so rows of 6 need only new strides
cat allocates and copies every pass; view allocates nothing
a view fails when the memory isn't in the needed order (e.g. after a transpose)

retrieve.q: Explain what a stride is, using a.view(9, 2) of torch.arange(18) as your example.
answer: strides are (2, 1): one step down a row skips 2 slots, one step across skips 1
element [i, j] lives at storage slot 2i + j
all views of a share the same 18-slot storage

retrieve.q: Walk through what PyTorch does when you call emb.view(-1, 6) on the (32, 3, 2) emb: what gets checked, what gets created, and what memory is touched.
answer: infers -1: 192 elements ÷ 6 = 32
checks the new shape can be expressed with strides over the existing layout (emb is contiguous with strides (6, 2, 1))
creates a new tensor header with shape (32, 6), strides (6, 1), same storage and offset
no numbers are read or copied

retrieve.q: You have a non-contiguous tensor and need it flattened to rows. Compare .view, .reshape and .contiguous().view: what does each cost, and how does each fail?
answer: .view: free, but raises a RuntimeError when the layout doesn't allow it
.reshape: always works, but may silently copy, so you can't count on shared memory
.contiguous().view: explicit copy first, then a free view; clear about the cost
and after a transpose, even a successful copy gives a different element order than the untransposed view

retrieve.q: In the final model C is (27, 10) and the code says emb.view(-1, 30). Why 30, and what would break if you kept view(-1, 6)?
answer: 30 = 3 context characters × 10 numbers each
view(-1, 6) would still succeed (960 ÷ 6 = 160 rows) but slice each example's 30 numbers into five wrong rows of 6
the matmul with W1 (30, 200) then fails on shape, which is how you'd notice

compare.q: Both C[X] and emb.view(-1, 6) produce a new tensor from an old one. Which one copies memory and which doesn't, what design choice causes it, and when would the difference matter?
answer: C[X] is advanced indexing: it gathers rows (repeating C[0] many times), so it must allocate a new (32, 3, 2) tensor; checked: it does not share C's memory
view only changes the header, so it shares emb's memory
a gather can't be described by strides when rows repeat or jump around; a reshape of contiguous memory can
it matters for memory at scale and for writes: editing emb never changes C, but editing a view changes emb

compare.q: Here view flattens all 3 characters into one row; in WaveNet a view groups consecutive pairs, (4, 8, 10) → (4, 4, 20). What is the same mechanism in both, and what new question does WaveNet's version raise?
answer: same: contiguous memory, only the strides change, so both are free
here the whole context is merged at once; WaveNet merges two neighbours at a time to build a tree
WaveNet's view puts characters 2k and 2k+1 side by side because they are adjacent in memory, which is why it equals torch.cat([e[:, ::2, :], e[:, 1::2, :]], dim=2) without the copy

predict.q: Instead of emb.view(-1, 6) you write emb.transpose(1, 2).view(-1, 6). What happens? And if you fix it with .contiguous() first, does row 0 still read 1.5674, -0.2373, 1.5674, -0.2373, 1.5674, -0.2373?
predict.answer: The view raises RuntimeError: view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride ...: the transpose made strides (6, 1, 2), so rows of 6 aren't contiguous. With .contiguous() it copies and succeeds, but row 0 becomes 1.5674, 1.5674, 1.5674, -0.2373, -0.2373, -0.2373: first all three characters' dimension 0, then all their dimension 1. Same numbers, different order, and the model would be wired differently (measured in the course venv).

apply.task: Switch to the final model's embedding size: C = torch.randn((27, 10), generator=g) with the same seed, and emb = C[X] for the first 5 words. Before running anything, write down emb.shape, emb.stride(), the strides of emb.view(-1, 30), and the storage slot of emb[4, 2, 7]. Then check all four, and confirm that emb.view(-1, 30)[4, 27] and emb.flatten()[slot] equal emb[4, 2, 7].
apply.done: You predicted (32, 3, 10), strides (30, 10, 1), view strides (30, 1), slot 4·30 + 2·10 + 7 = 147, and all three reads give the same number (−1.6261 with seed 2147483647).
apply.hint: Strides of a contiguous tensor are the products of the sizes to the right: 3·10 = 30, then 10, then 1.
